title: Use language and communication in occupational learning programmes

lessons.title: Language for learning at work
lessons.html:
Why language matters in training

In an occupational learning programme you learn by reading manuals, listening to facilitators, taking part in group work, keeping a portfolio of evidence and writing assessments. Strong language skills help you understand, take part and show what you know.

Listening and speaking in learning

  • Listen for key words, steps and safety warnings in demonstrations, for example how to tack up a horse or mix a dip.
  • Ask questions when something is unclear. There are no stupid questions in training.
  • Take part in group discussions and give reasons for your answers.
  • Explain a procedure in your own words to check that you understand it.

Reading learning material

  1. Preview: read headings, pictures and summaries first.
  2. Read for meaning: underline key words and new terms.
  3. Build vocabulary: keep a glossary of technical words, like "farrier", "withers", "biosecurity" or "dosage", with meanings in your own language.
  4. Read instructions carefully: labels, SOPs and assessment questions. Look for command words such as list, describe, explain and compare.
  5. Read tables and diagrams: such as a feed chart or vaccination schedule.
Command wordWhat it asks you to do
ListGive items, no explanation
DescribeSay what something looks like or how it happens
ExplainGive reasons, say why
CompareShow how things are the same and different

lessons.title: Writing and using information in your learning
lessons.html:
Writing in learning programmes

You will write answers, reports, logbook entries and reflections. Good writing is clear, correct and organised.

Steps for writing

  1. Plan: what is the purpose and who will read it? Jot down main points.
  2. Draft: write in short paragraphs, one main idea each.
  3. Check: spelling, punctuation, and that you answered the question.
  4. Final copy: neat and complete, with your name and date.

Logbooks and workplace records

A logbook entry should say what you did, when, where, with which animal or equipment, and what you learnt. Example: "14 March, Stable 3: Picked out the hooves of the bay mare Lady. Found a stone in the left fore. Removed it and told the supervisor."

Finding and using information

  • Use manuals, the facilitator, colleagues, labels and reliable websites.
  • Check that information is current and from a trusted source.
  • Write information in your own words. Copying someone else's work is plagiarism and is not allowed in assessments.

Preparing for assessment

  • Know what evidence you need for your portfolio.
  • Ask the assessor to explain anything you do not understand.
  • You have the right to appeal an assessment decision if you think it was unfair.

Key points

  • Listen for key steps and safety warnings and ask questions.
  • Preview, read for meaning and keep a glossary of new words.
  • Understand command words such as list, describe, explain and compare.
  • Plan, draft and check your writing.
  • Use reliable sources and your own words; plagiarism is not allowed.
